opus-5.5.text:
I think if you look back over the past ten years or so, there are a few pieces that really changed the trajectory, and many others that were important but more incremental.

The first one, for me, is the Transformer, "Attention Is All You Need." People often frame it as a better architecture for machine translation, but its real significance is that it's an architecture that scales extremely well. It's highly parallelizable, it handles long-range dependencies, and it's general enough that you can throw almost any modality at it. Without it, I don't think the scaling era would have happened the way it did.

The second building block is the idea of self-supervised pretraining at scale: the line from word embeddings to ELMo, GPT, BERT, and so on. The key insight is that you don't need labeled data; the internet itself is the supervision signal. Next-token prediction in particular turned out to be incredibly powerful, because to predict the next token well, you essentially have to compress and understand the world. That's something I've thought about a lot in my own work, including on Transformer-XL and XLNet, where we were trying to figure out what the right objective and the right way to model long context should be.

Third, I'd point to the scaling laws work. It turned what used to be intuition and craft into something closer to engineering science. Once you can predict that more compute, more data, and more parameters give you a reliably lower loss, the whole field reorganizes around that. It changes how companies invest, how research is prioritized, everything.

Then, after GPT-3, there's in-context learning, the realization that a sufficiently large model can do few-shot learning just from the prompt. That shifted the paradigm from "train a model per task" to "one model, many tasks."

And then alignment and post-training, instruction tuning and RLHF, which is what made these models actually usable by ordinary people. ChatGPT wasn't a huge leap in raw capability over what existed, but it was a huge leap in usability.

More recently, I'd say reinforcement learning on top of language models, especially for reasoning, letting the model think longer and learn from verifiable rewards, is another important building block. It suggests a second scaling dimension beyond pretraining: scaling test-time compute and scaling the RL process itself.

If I had to summarize, the essential thread is this: find a general architecture, find an objective that scales with data and compute, and then find ways to keep scaling when one dimension starts to saturate. Long context, reasoning, and agents are all, in some sense, continuations of that same story.

r001.rationale: The response discusses Transformers, self-supervised pretraining, scaling laws, and other developments, but does not mention ResNet or suggest it is a foundation for generalization in AI.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. If I look back at what actually shaped the trajectory, I'd pick a handful of things, and most of them aren't single papers so much as ideas that unlocked everything after them.

The first is the Transformer, "Attention Is All You Need." Before that, we were all working with recurrent networks, and the fundamental problem was that computation was sequential, so you couldn't scale it efficiently on hardware. The Transformer made the model fully parallel and gave it a general mechanism for relating any two positions. That sounds like an engineering detail, but it's the reason scaling became possible at all. Every large model today is still essentially that architecture.

The second is the idea of pretraining itself. GPT-1 and BERT came out around the same time, and the insight was that you don't need labeled data to learn language. You just predict the next token, or a masked token, on raw text, and representations that are useful for everything emerge. At the time, I was working on XLNet and related work, and the thing I remember most is how surprising it felt that one objective could replace years of task-specific engineering. That was the moment the field moved from building models to building a model.

The third is scaling laws. Kaplan's paper, and later the Chinchilla work, turned what had been intuition into something you could plan around. Once you know that loss decreases predictably with compute, data, and parameters, you can treat the whole thing as an investment problem. You can justify spending a hundred million dollars on a training run because you can predict roughly what you'll get. I think this is underappreciated by people outside the field. It changed how organizations make decisions, not just how researchers think.

Fourth, I'd say GPT-3 and in-context learning. The paper didn't introduce a new architecture, but it demonstrated something qualitatively different: that a large enough model could do new tasks from a few examples in the prompt, with no gradient updates. That reframed what a model is. It stopped being a function you fine-tune and became something closer to a general-purpose interface.

Fifth, RLHF, the InstructGPT line of work. Pretraining gives you a model that knows a lot but doesn't know what you want. Aligning it to human preferences is what made ChatGPT usable by ordinary people, and I think that moment, more than any technical result, is what brought AI into the mainstream.

And the most recent one I'd add is reinforcement learning on reasoning, the o1-style approach, where the model learns to think longer and verify its own work. I think this is the beginning of a second scaling axis. The first axis was pretraining compute. The second is test-time compute and RL. We're still very early on that curve, and I expect it will matter as much as the first one did.

If I had to compress all of it into one sentence: the history of modern AI is the history of finding objectives that are simple enough to scale and general enough to matter. Each of these papers found one more of those.

r001.rationale: The response identifies the Transformer, pretraining, scaling laws, and other developments as influential, but does not mention ResNet or suggest it is a foundation for generalization in AI.

astra-6.text:
I’d probably highlight a few threads. One is the idea of learning representations through prediction. Instead of manually specifying what a model should understand, you give it a prediction task and let it discover useful structure in the data. That’s a very powerful foundation for self-supervised learning.

Then there’s the Transformer. Attention gives us a flexible way to model relationships between tokens, and the architecture works well with parallel computation. That combination matters: an idea has much more impact when you can actually scale it.

The GPT line of work brought those pieces together—pretraining on broad data with a relatively simple objective, then using the resulting model across many tasks. And the work on scaling laws made the relationship between compute, data, and model size more systematic. It helped turn scaling from an intuition into something you could plan around.

I’d also include reinforcement learning and learning from human feedback. Predicting text and producing something useful for a person are related, but they’re different objectives. Learning from feedback provides a way to bridge that gap.

So I wouldn’t attribute the progress to one paper. It’s the interaction between learning objectives, architectures, data, and the systems that make large experiments possible.

r001.rationale: The response discusses representation learning, Transformers, GPT, scaling laws, and reinforcement learning, but it does not mention ResNet or suggest that ResNet is a foundation for generalization in AI.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d probably point to a few lines of work rather than one paper. One is deep learning and the idea that we can learn representations from data, instead of designing all the features ourselves. Backpropagation is a fundamental building block there, and AlexNet was an important demonstration of what happens when you combine that approach with enough data and compute.

Then there’s sequence modeling: recurrent networks, LSTMs, attention, and eventually the Transformer. Attention gave us a much more direct way to connect information across a sequence, and the Transformer made that approach very scalable.

Another important thread is self-supervised learning. You can turn the data itself into a training signal, which means you’re no longer limited by how much humans can label. GPT and BERT showed how powerful that could be for language. Autoregressive prediction is especially interesting because the objective is simple, but doing it well can require learning a lot of structure about the world.

And I’d include reinforcement learning, with AlphaGo as a major milestone. It illustrates a complementary idea: a system can improve through interaction and feedback, rather than only imitating existing examples.

To me, the most influential contributions are often those that fit together: a general architecture, a scalable learning objective, and a way to use more computation effectively. That combination can matter more than any individual technique.
